title: The Complete CFD Engineer
subtitle: Cracking the CFD Interview — From First Principles to Job-Ready
author: Subramanian J H

chapters.title: Foundations: Mathematics & Fluid Mechanics for CFD
chapters.objective: Build the mathematical and physical intuition every CFD engineer needs so that the equations, meshes and solver settings later in the book feel like extensions of ideas you already understand.
chapters.summary: This chapter grounds you in the vector calculus, linear algebra and fluid-mechanics fundamentals that CFD is built on. You will learn how fields, derivatives and conservation laws describe a flowing fluid, how the governing PDEs are classified, and how flow behaviour is visualised and categorised. Every topic ties back to what actually happens inside a CFD solver and in real automotive engineering work.

topics.title: Scalars, Vectors, Tensors and Fields
concept: A scalar is a quantity with magnitude only (temperature T, pressure p, density rho). A vector has magnitude and direction (velocity V, force F) and needs multiple components, e.g. V = (u, v, w). A tensor generalises this: a second-order tensor like the stress tensor has a magnitude and TWO associated directions, giving nine components in 3D.
A field means a quantity defined at every point in space (and possibly time). So a temperature field T(x,y,z,t) gives one number per point, while a velocity field V(x,y,z,t) gives a vector per point.
Rule of thumb: scalar = 1 number, vector = 3 numbers (3D), 2nd-order tensor = 9 numbers.
why: CFD solves for fields, not single values: the solver stores a scalar or vector at every cell. Knowing the order of a quantity tells you how many equations and how much memory it needs. Stress and strain-rate are tensors, which is exactly why the momentum equation is more involved than a heat equation.
usecases: Storing velocity, pressure and temperature fields across millions of mesh cells.
The viscous stress tensor in the Navier-Stokes momentum equation.
Post-processing contour plots (scalar fields) versus vector/streamline plots.
Reporting drag as a vector force resolved from a surface stress tensor on a car body.
everyday: Temperature on a weather map is a scalar field - one number per city.
Wind arrows on that same map are a vector field - speed and direction.
Squeezing a sponge in different directions at once is tensor-like stress.
topics.tip: When you see nine components or 'two directions', think tensor - and remember stress and strain-rate are the tensors that make the momentum equation harder than a scalar transport equation.
qa: What is the difference between a vector and a tensor?

A vector has a magnitude and a single direction (3 components in 3D). A second-order tensor associates a magnitude with two directions (9 components), like stress, which needs a face orientation and a force direction.
How many components does the stress tensor have in 3D?
Nine (a 3x3 matrix). Because it is symmetric for most fluids, only six are independent.
What is a 'field' in CFD?
A quantity defined at every point in the domain, such as p(x,y,z,t) or V(x,y,z,t). CFD discretises the domain and stores the field values at each cell or node.
Is pressure a scalar or a vector?
Pressure is a scalar - it has magnitude only. The force it produces on a surface is a vector, equal to pressure times area acting normal to the surface.
Why does representing stress as a tensor matter for the Navier-Stokes equations?

Because momentum transfer by viscosity depends on how each velocity component varies in each direction; only a tensor captures all those gradient combinations, producing the viscous term in the momentum equation.

topics.title: Gradient, Divergence, Curl and the Laplacian
concept: These are the core differential operators of CFD, all built from the del operator ∇. Gradient (∇T) acts on a scalar and returns a vector pointing toward the steepest increase - it drives diffusion and pressure forces. Divergence (∇·V) acts on a vector and returns a scalar measuring net outflow per unit volume; ∇·V = 0 means incompressible.

Curl (∇×V) acts on a vector and returns a vector measuring local rotation (vorticity). The Laplacian (∇²T = ∇·∇T) is the divergence of a gradient, a scalar that measures how a value differs from its surroundings - the heart of diffusion.
Memory aid: gradient makes vectors from scalars, divergence makes scalars from vectors, curl makes vectors from vectors.
why: Every term in the governing equations is one of these operators. Pressure gradient drives flow, divergence enforces mass conservation, curl quantifies vortices behind cars and wings, and the Laplacian models viscous and thermal diffusion. Understanding them lets you read the Navier-Stokes equations physically instead of as symbols.
usecases: ∇·V = 0 as the incompressibility constraint solved in the pressure-velocity coupling.
Vorticity (∇×V) contours to visualise wake and tip vortices on a vehicle or wing.
The Laplacian ∇²V representing viscous diffusion of momentum.
Pressure-gradient ∇p driving the flow in the momentum equation.
everyday: Gradient: walking downhill, you naturally move opposite the steepest slope of the terrain.
Divergence: air rushing out of a punctured balloon spreads outward from a source.
Curl: a leaf spinning in a small whirlpool shows local rotation of the water.
topics.tip: Read the Navier-Stokes equation term by term - spot the pressure gradient, the divergence and the Laplacian, and the whole equation becomes a physical story rather than algebra.
qa: What does ∇·V = 0 physically mean?
Zero divergence means no net mass is created or destroyed in any volume - inflow equals outflow. For constant-density flow this is the incompressibility condition.
What is the difference between gradient and divergence?

Gradient operates on a scalar and produces a vector (direction of steepest rise). Divergence operates on a vector and produces a scalar (net outflow rate). They also differ in the type of input and output.
What is vorticity and how is it computed?
Vorticity is the curl of the velocity field, ω = ∇×V. It measures the local rate of rotation of fluid elements and is high in shear layers, wakes and vortex cores.
Where does the Laplacian appear in the Navier-Stokes equations?
In the viscous term, μ∇²V, which represents diffusion of momentum. It also appears in the pressure Poisson equation, ∇²p = source.
If curl of velocity is zero everywhere, what do we call the flow?
Irrotational flow. It permits a velocity potential (V = ∇φ) and underlies potential-flow theory used for quick aerodynamic estimates.

mcqs.q: How many independent components does the symmetric stress tensor have in 3D?
mcqs.exp: A second-order tensor has 9 components (3x3), but symmetry for most fluids leaves only 6 independent.

mcqs.q: Which statement about pressure is correct?
options: Pressure is a vector because it has direction
Pressure is a scalar; the force it exerts on a surface is a vector
mcqs.exp: Pressure has magnitude only (scalar); multiplying by area and surface normal yields a force vector.

mcqs.q: What does a 'field' mean in CFD?
options: A single averaged value for the whole domain
Only boundary values of a variable
A quantity defined at every point in the domain, e.g. V(x,y,z,t)
mcqs.exp: A field assigns a value (scalar or vector) to every point in space and time, which the solver stores per cell.

mcqs.q: The gradient operator acts on a scalar and produces:
options: A vector pointing toward steepest increase
mcqs.exp: Gradient makes a vector from a scalar, pointing in the direction of steepest rise.

options: No net mass created or destroyed; incompressible flow
mcqs.exp: Zero divergence means inflow equals outflow in any volume, the incompressible condition.
